card.title: Elementary Idea of the Quantum Mechanical Model — de Broglie's Wave Equation

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: de Broglie (1924) turned Bohr's postulate into physics: every moving particle has wavelength λ = h/mv, so an orbiting electron is a wave that survives only when a whole number of wavelengths fits its circumference (2πr = nλ) — which rearranges exactly to Bohr's mvr = nh/2π. Davisson and Germer (1927) proved it by diffracting electrons off nickel.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - λ = h/mv = h/p (de Broglie) - Standing wave: 2πr = nλ → mvr = nh/2π (Bohr recovered) - h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg - Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π (why orbitals replace orbits)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **ψ vs ψ²:** ψ has no physical interpretation; ψ² is the probability density. Never interchange them.  ·  **Orbit vs orbital:** orbit = Bohr's fixed circular track; orbital = quantum probability region. The words differ by one letter and one revolution of meaning.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The electron is not a particle on a track but a wave of probability: where the wave is strong, the electron is likely to be found."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Electron at 10⁶ m/s → λ ≈ 0.73 nm*** — atomic-scale wavelength, so nickel crystals (spacing ~ nm) diffract it; a cricket ball at 40 m/s gives λ ≈ 10⁻³⁴ m — 20 orders too small to ever observe.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Matter Learns to Wave Bohr postulated quantisation; de Broglie (1924) **derived** it. If light — a wave — can behave as particles (photoelectric effect), then particles — electrons — should behave as waves. An electron wave can circle the nucleus only if a **whole number of wavelengths fits the orbit**; that condition *is* Bohr's quantisation, no longer arbitrary.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The de Broglie relation Every moving particle has a wavelength: **λ = h / mv = h / p** (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) - For **macroscopic** objects m is large → λ is absurdly small → wave nature is undetectable. - For an **electron** (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at ordinary speeds λ ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m — atomic dimensions — so wave behaviour shows. ### 2.2 Deriving Bohr's quantisation (the 3m chain) 1.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "λ = h over mv — small m, big λ." Derivation chain: standing wave → 2πr = nλ → substitute → mvr = nh/2π. Davisson–Germer = the proof name to drop.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): State de Broglie's relation and calculate the wavelength of an electron moving at 10⁶ m s⁻¹.** — λ = h/mv = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁶) = **7.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m ≈ 0.73 nm**. The relation asserts that every moving particle has a wave character with λ inversely proportional to its momentum.  ·  **NEB-style (3m): Derive Bohr's quantisation condition from de Broglie's hypothesis.** — (1) For a stable orbit the electron wave must be a standing wave: 2πr = nλ. (2) Substituting λ = h/mv: 2πr = nh/mv. (3) Rearranging: mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's postulate of quantised angular momentum, now a consequence of wave geometry.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: In numericals keep h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg; quote λ in nm for electrons. For the derivation, write all three steps — NEB awards each line.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Quantisation becomes geometry:** only orbits fitting a whole number of electron wavelengths are self-reinforcing standing waves — Bohr's rule is a consequence, not a postulate.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: λ = h/mv (de Broglie, 1924); standing-wave condition 2πr = nλ derives Bohr's mvr = nh/2π; Davisson–Germer (1927) proved electron diffraction off nickel; Schrödinger's wave equation yields orbitals = ψ² probability regions; electron λ ~ 10⁻¹⁰ m (observable), macroscopic λ ~ 10⁻³⁴ m (unobservable).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Electron microscopes exploit the electron's short de Broglie wavelength (~picometres at high voltage) to image far beyond the diffraction limit of light microscopes.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Describe the Davisson–Germer experiment and its conclusion.** — Electrons accelerated onto a **nickel crystal** produced a **diffraction pattern** (like X-rays), proving electrons behave as waves; the measured wavelength agreed with λ = h/mv.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Why does the quantum mechanical model replace orbits with orbitals?** — Because Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π forbids knowing the electron's exact path; the Schrödinger equation instead gives ψ, and ψ² maps the **probability** of finding the electron — a 3-D orbital, not a track.

rows.text: What does the Davisson–Germer experiment establish that the photoelectric effect does not?  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **ψ vs ψ²:** ψ is the wave function (no direct physical meaning); **ψ² is the probability density** — the measurable one. Quoting ψ as "probability" loses the mark.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Diffraction vs scattering:** diffraction is wave-bending around/through regular arrays (needs wavelength ~ spacing); scattering is any direction change. Davisson–Germer is diffraction — the wave proof.  ·  **de Broglie applies to everything:** the relation is universal; for cricket balls λ is simply too small to matter. Saying "large objects have no wavelength" is wrong — they have unobservable ones.  ·  ## 7. Exam Application **NEB-style (2m): State the de Broglie relation and its significance.** — λ = h/mv: every moving particle has a wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum. It explains why microscopic particles show wave behaviour and derives Bohr's quantisation (2πr = nλ → mvr = nh/2π).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Show that Bohr's quantisation condition follows from de Broglie's hypothesis.** — The electron wave on a stationary orbit must be a standing wave: 2πr = nλ. With λ = h/mv: 2πr = nh/mv → mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's postulate of quantised angular momentum, now derived rather than decreed.  ·  **NEB-style (2m): An electron and a cricket ball move at the same speed. Which has the longer wavelength and why?** — The electron: λ = h/mv, so the smaller mass (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg vs 0.15 kg) gives the larger λ — electron λ ~ nm scale (observable), ball λ ~ 10⁻³⁴ m (unobservable).
